meta: Anders Zorn's 1893 portrait of Bertha Palmer with the ivory gavel she used to chair the Board of Lady Managers in Chicago.
about: Bertha Palmer holds the ivory gavel she used to preside over the Board of Lady Managers for the World's Columbian Exposition in Chicago. The board, with Palmer as president, organized the Woman's Building at the fair. She asked the Swedish painter Anders Zorn for the portrait because his impressionistic style suited her taste as a collector, which was thought radical then. Palmer commissioned it in 1893, and her family gave it to the Art Institute in 1922.

meta: A courtesan beneath a mosquito net with her cat, a hanging scroll of 1855 by Utagawa Kunisada that plays on The Tale of Genji.
about: A courtesan in a blue kimono rises from beneath a mosquito net while her small white cat looks back at her. The museum reads the scene as a nod to The Tale of Genji. There a cat pushes aside a bamboo blind and reveals the Third Princess to the courtier Kashiwagi, and a secret affair begins. Comparisons between court literature and city life, called mitate, were a popular device in Edo art. A poem by Honda Jinzaburo at the top mentions the Omi vendors of mosquito nets and the trysts of courtesans under them on steamy summer nights.

meta: Arion on a Sea Horse and Bacchante on a Panther, a pair of 1855 paintings by William Adolphe Bouguereau on gold grounds.
about: These two paintings belong to a series of eight that Bouguereau made for a Parisian home decorated in the style of the wall paintings found at Pompeii. The Greek poet Arion escaped pirates on the back of a sea creature drawn by his singing. In the companion picture a bacchante, a follower of Bacchus, rides a panther and carries a spear tipped with a pinecone. Both figures stand out against a gold honeycomb background that echoes Roman mosaics Bouguereau had studied in Italy. The soft flesh tones and gold leaf were meant to come alive under the mansion's gas lighting.

meta: A Greater Morning, a 1900 painting by Arthur B. Davies of two nudes at dawn who recall Adam and Eve.
about: Two figures stand in the soft light of an early dawn. The museum says they recall Adam and Eve in the Garden of Eden, unaware of their nudity and waking to a new beginning in an untouched world. Arthur B. Davies painted many nude women in dramatic landscapes early in his career. Like many artists around 1900, he answered the country's growing urbanization with idealized images of people in harmony with nature.

meta: A Storm on a Mediterranean Coast, Claude-Joseph Vernet's 1767 view of a shipwreck's aftermath beneath a lighthouse.
about: Claude-Joseph Vernet painted the aftermath of a storm. Dark clouds hang over an angry sea, a wrecked boat lies on the shore with its anxious survivors, and ships list in the distance. The Getty points to the strong opposing diagonals of the waves, the rain shaft in the distance, the battered ship and even the fleeing castaways. The lighthouse at the center stands upright against all that motion. Waves burst into white foam beyond the rocks.

meta: Expectation, a mural by Richard Roland Holst made for an interior by Berlage shown at the Leipzig building exhibition of 1913.
about: A naked man runs and shoots an arrow from his bow, with a dog at his feet. Stylized waves and birds fill the background. Richard Roland Holst made this wall painting for an interior by Berlage that was shown at the building exhibition in Leipzig in 1913. He kept it, and the work was bequeathed to the Dutch State in 1938 along with other objects. It was transferred to the Rijksmuseum in 1979.

meta: Breezing Up, Winslow Homer's picture of four boys in the sailboat Gloucester, which the National Gallery of Art bought in 1943.
about: Four boys ride in a small open sailboat named Gloucester. It heels over as it cuts through choppy green water under a cloudy sky, and a schooner sails far off at the right. Charles Stewart Smith of New York owned the painting by 1878. His son believed his father bought it straight from Winslow Homer. The gallery notes that Smith may instead have bought it at auction in early 1877. The son sold it in 1943 to Wildenstein, and the National Gallery bought it on 31 December of that year.
credit_line: Gift of the W. L. and May T. Mellon Foundation

meta: See-non-ty-a, an Iowa medicine man painted by George Catlin in 1844 and 1845, given to the National Gallery of Art in 1965.
about: The sitter wears a tall red-tipped feathered headdress, layered beaded necklaces, a large white shell pendant and long fringed earrings. His face is painted red. George Catlin kept the portrait until his death, and it passed to his three daughters. In 1912 the American Museum of Natural History bought it from Elizabeth Wing Catlin. Kennedy Galleries sold it in 1959 to Paul Mellon, who gave it to the National Gallery of Art in 1965.

meta: Salisbury Cathedral from Lower Marsh Close, a 1820 painting by John Constable that stayed unsold in his lifetime.
about: The spire of Salisbury Cathedral rises over a broad green meadow, framed at the left by large dark trees. Loose, feathery brushwork renders the billowing clouds. Constable never sold the painting. It went under the hammer at his sale in London in 1838, together with Glebe Farm, and William Hooker Carpenter bought it. Later owners included Sir John Kelk. Dealers handled it in New York, and William K. Bixby of St. Louis bought it after the sale to Arthur Tooth and Son in 1903.

meta: The Loge, Mary Cassatt's picture of two young women in a theater box, bought from the artist by Durand-Ruel in 1896.
about: Two young women sit side by side in a theater box, one partly hidden behind a lace-patterned fan with pink flowers. The woman in front wears an off-shoulder white gown, long gloves and a dark choker. Durand-Ruel bought the painting from the artist in April 1896. It went to Baron de Herzog in 1911 and then to the Budapest collector Marczell von Nemes. His sale in Paris in 1913 followed. Chester Dale bought it from Paul Rosenberg, and it came to the National Gallery of Art by his bequest in 1963.

meta: Gerhard van Suchtelen, painted by Gerard ter Borch the Younger about 1666 and acquired by the National Gallery of Art in 2014.
about: A standing man with long reddish hair wears a black cloak over a dark doublet and a large lace collar. His black hat rests on a table beside him under a pink cloth fringed in gold. An inscription on the back names him as Gerhard van Suchtelen, burgomaster of Deventer and son of Abraham van Suchtelen. The painting was in London in 1882. William A. Clark of New York owned it later, and he left it to the Corcoran Gallery of Art in 1926. The National Gallery of Art acquired it in 2014.

meta: View of Dordrecht from the Dordtse Kil, Jan van Goyen's river scene signed in 1644 on the stern of a boat.
about: Sailing and rowing boats crowded with figures fill a broad river under a pale, cloudy sky. A fisherman works on the left bank, and a church tower and a row of buildings rise along the far shore. Jan van Goyen signed it on the stern of a boat. In 1906 it was sold to Baron Vladimir de Gunzburg in Paris, and his son Serge de Gunzburg of Geneva inherited it. The National Gallery of Art bought it in 1978 through the Heim Gallery.

meta: Gustave Courbet's 1857 portrait of a young girl, bequeathed by Chester Dale to the National Gallery of Art in 1963.
about: A young girl turns slightly toward the viewer in a wide-brimmed brown hat with a fabric flower, a dark cape with frogged buttons and a white collar. Behind her the ground is pale and loosely brushed. Courbet signed and dated it at the lower left. Gustave Cahen of Paris owned the painting, and it appeared in his 1929 sale as a portrait of a young woman. Chester Dale acquired it, possibly through Etienne Bignou, and bequeathed it to the gallery in 1963.

meta: Edgar Degas's self-portrait with a white collar, painted about 1857 and given to the National Gallery of Art in 1995.
about: A young man's head and shoulders emerge from a dark brown ground, his face warmly lit. A bright white collar stands out beneath a dark jacket and loosely tied cravat. Degas kept the picture. It came to his nephew Edmond Degas, and an inscription on the stretcher says it was not sold with the studio and was bought from the nephew. The collector Marcel Guérin had it by 1924, when he lent it to a Paris show. Paul Mellon bought it in 1959, and it came to the gallery in 1995.
credit_line: Collection of Mr. and Mrs. Paul Mellon

meta: Moon of Enlightenment, a hanging scroll by Tsukioka Yoshitoshi from the series Twelve Aspects of the Moon, given to the Art Institute of Chicago in 2018.
about: A heavy, bald monk in a white robe reclines and points upward at a pale full moon. A green fan with gold detailing lies near his side. The scroll is painted in ink and color on silk. It was recorded in 1963 with Kaneko Fusui in Japan and later with Nakau Ei, who still had it in 1992. Christie's sold it in New York on 18 May 2007 to Roger Weston of Chicago. He gave it away. The Art Institute received the gift in 2018.

meta: Landscape with Two Poplars, Vasily Kandinsky's 1912 painting, sold in 1913 to the Chicago collector Arthur Jerome Eddy.
about: Tall, dark tree forms rise above a yellow path that curves through a field of green and red. Patches of blue, orange and brown fill the hills and buildings around it. Kandinsky sold the painting in 1913 to the Chicago collector Arthur Jerome Eddy. After Eddy died in 1920, it passed to his wife Lucy and his son Jerome, who gave it to the Art Institute of Chicago in 1931. Look at the yellow path.
